chief_complaint: pain on inner elbow when wrist is flexed against resistance
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain on inner elbow when wrist is flexed against resistance. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she strained the inner part of her arm from carrying heavy bags of groceries and lifting heavy cookware.
concerns: She is worried that the arm pain will become permanent and prevent her from safely lifting and caring for her infant grandchild.
expectations: She hopes to get prescribed strong pain relief patches and advice on how to rest her arm without stopping all her daily chores.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Medial Epicondylitis: Elbow strap, forearm stretching, modify hand mechanics, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: pain on inner elbow when wrist is flexed against resistance

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain on inner elbow when wrist is flexed against resistance. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Medial Epicondylitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Numbness in the ring/little finger would suggest ulnar nerve involvement rather than pure epicondylitis.
management_principles: Plan for Medial Epicondylitis: Elbow strap, forearm stretching, modify hand mechanics
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.objective: Characterize the pain location and triggers
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does resisted wrist flexion cause it?
Do you have any numbness or tingling in your ring or little finger?
What activities involve gripping or throwing motions for you, like golf?
How long has this been bothering you?

must_ask.objective: Explain the bracing and stretching plan
must_ask.say: We recommend an elbow strap, forearm stretching, and modifying your hand mechanics.

history.answer: I have been having this pain on the inside of my right elbow for the past three weeks, especially whenever I bend my wrist inward.
The pain is located right on the bony bump on the inner side of my right elbow, and my left elbow feels completely normal.
It started gradually about three weeks ago, and over the last few days it has become progressively worse.
It is a dull, aching soreness at rest that turns into a sharp pain, about a 6 out of 10, when I grip or bend my wrist.
No, I have not noticed any swelling, redness, or heat around the elbow joint.
No, I do not have any morning stiffness in my elbow or hands when I wake up.
It gets much worse when I bend my wrist inward, lift grocery bags, or wring out wet towels, and it calms down when I rest it.
I recently started playing golf twice a week, and I also spent the last month doing heavy gardening and repotting heavy flowerpots.
I find it difficult to hold a heavy frying pan or turn tight door handles with my right hand, but I can manage my other daily chores.
No, I do not have any numbness, tingling, or prickling sensations in my ring or little finger.
No, my neck does not hurt and the pain does not shoot down from my neck or shoulder.
No, I have not had any fever or chills at all.
No, I did not bump, twist, or injure my arm, and I haven't heard any popping sounds or felt the joint lock.
No, I have never experienced this kind of elbow pain in my life.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and more worn out than usual recently, but I have not had any fevers or weight loss.
No, I have not had any skin rashes, mouth ulcers, hair loss, eye redness, or dry mouth.
No, I do not have morning back stiffness, heel pain, or swelling in my fingers or toes.
No, I have not had any diarrhea, burning during urination, discharge, or sore throats recently.
I only have an occasional glass of wine and have not changed my diet, and I do not take water pills.
No, I have never had steroid injections, joint surgery, artificial joints, or medications that lower immunity.
I have been married to my husband for over thirty years and we have no other sexual partners.
I thought I strained something on the inside of my elbow from lugging heavy grocery bags and cast-iron pots.
I'm worried this pain won't go away and I won't be able to carry or babysit my new grandbaby safely.
I'm hoping to get some medicated pain patches and practical advice on how to let my elbow rest while still getting things done.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or arthritis.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain pills, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I am a retired elementary school teacher living at home with my husband.
No one in my family has had rheumatoid arthritis, gout, or autoimmune joint disorders.

exam.finding: Alert 62-year-old female in no acute distress, resting her right forearm comfortably.
Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Marked point tenderness over the right medial epicondyle and common flexor origin; full active and passive elbow range of motion without effusion, warmth, erythema, or cubital tunnel tenderness.
Pain reproduced over the right medial epicondyle during resisted wrist flexion and pronation; motor strength is 5/5 throughout bilateral upper extremities.
Intact light touch sensation across bilateral upper extremities, including the fourth and fifth digits in the ulnar nerve distribution.
Biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis reflexes are 2+ bilaterally and symmetric; negative Hoffman sign.
Full and pain-free cervical spine range of motion without midline tenderness; Spurling test is negative bilaterally.
No skin rash, psoriatic plaques, tophi, rheumatoid nodules, or nail pitting on inspection.
Normal, steady gait with coordinated reciprocal arm swing.
